content.overview: Injuria sine damno means infringement of a legal right without consequential loss and can be actionable; damnum sine injuria means loss without infringement of a legal right and is ordinarily not actionable.
content.glance: Injuria sine damno means infringement of a legal right without consequential loss and can be actionable; damnum sine injuria means loss without infringement of a legal right and is ordinarily not actionable.
content.study: Injuria sine damno means infringement of a legal right without consequential loss and can be actionable; damnum sine injuria means loss without infringement of a legal right and is ordinarily not actionable.\n\nThe distinction protects legal rights without making every economic loss compensable. Ashby v White illustrates actionable infringement without measurable financial loss, while Gloucester Grammar School illustrates lawful competition causing loss without a tort. The court must identify the underlying right rather than rely on the maxim alone.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: The distinction protects legal rights without making every economic loss compensable. Ashby v White illustrates actionable infringement without measurable financial loss, while Gloucester Grammar School illustrates lawful competition causing loss without a tort. The court must identify the underlying right rather than rely on the maxim alone.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: Neither maxim is a free-standing cause of action. The claimant must identify the legal right and the rule protecting it. Some torts are actionable per se; others require proof of actual damage.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Identify the legal right. 2. Prove its infringement where injuria is alleged. 3. If only loss is shown, identify an independent cause of action. 4. Separate existence of liability from quantification of damages.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Proof focuses first on the protected right and its invasion. Civil proof is generally on the balance of probabilities. Economic-loss claims often require documentary evidence of causation and quantum.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: The claim must disclose the specific legal right and cause of action. Limitation follows the underlying action. Statutory rights should be analysed under their own remedial scheme.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: A legal right may be actionable without consequential loss, while lawful conduct causing loss is not necessarily a tort. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Some torts are actionable without proof of consequential damage. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.

distinctions.title: Injuria sine damno vs Damnum sine injuria
distinctions.left: Injuria Sine Damno & Damnum Sine Injuria
distinctions.right: The former is infringement of a legal right without consequential loss; the latter is consequential loss without infringement of a legal right.

rows.left: A legal right may be actionable without consequential loss, while lawful conduct causing loss is not necessarily a tort.
rows.right: The former is infringement of a legal right without consequential loss; the latter is consequential loss without infringement of a legal right.

rows.left: Apply the ingredients of the pleaded tort.
rows.right: Do not substitute the neighbouring cause of action.

misconceptions.correction: Some torts are actionable without proof of consequential damage.

cases.name: Ashby v White
cases.facts: Ashby, a qualified voter, was prevented from casting his vote at an election. The case is associated with the proposition that infringement of a legal right may constitute actionable injury even without proof of financial loss.
cases.issue: Whether a qualified elector could maintain an action where his vote was wrongfully refused and no specific financial loss was shown.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The case is a leading historical authority associated with injuria sine damno: infringement of a legal right may be actionable notwithstanding absence of consequential financial loss. The reported litigation and later treatment of Holt CJ's reasoning should be read with care when describing the precise procedural and remedial basis.
cases.holding: The litigation concerned wrongful refusal of a qualified elector's vote and is commonly cited for the injuria sine damno principle.
cases.relevance: Use this historical authority to illustrate legal injury without consequential financial loss; verify the precise procedural history and remedial proposition before relying on it for a specific modern cause of action.

cases.name: Gloucester Grammar School Case
cases.facts: A schoolmaster established a rival grammar school in Gloucester, causing students to leave the plaintiff's school and reducing the plaintiff's income. The reported authority is used to illustrate loss caused by lawful competition without infringement of a protected legal right.
cases.issue: Whether economic loss caused by lawful competition, without infringement of a legal right, gives rise to an action.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Mere economic loss caused by lawful competition is not, without infringement of a legal right, sufficient to found the tort claim described by the maxim damnum sine injuria.
cases.holding: The rival schoolmaster was not liable merely because lawful competition caused the plaintiff economic loss.
cases.relevance: Use the historical authority to distinguish consequential economic loss from infringement of a legal right.
